deck.brief: Assess why Emirates remains the strongest all-round airline system in the Gulf despite established rivals and operating new entrants, and what must hold through the next decade.
deck.question: Is Emirates still the strongest all-round airline system in the Gulf, and what must hold for it to keep the lead through the next decade?
deck.answer: Emirates has the strongest all-round Gulf system today, with the lead conditional on Dubai recovery, premium-yield durability and aircraft delivery.

cover.subtitle: Why the Dubai system leads Gulf aviation despite incumbents and new players

pages.why: The opening states the answer and the four conditions it rests on, with the evidence for each pillar in one table
pages.adds: Each point names the condition under which its pillar keeps holding, which the evidence column alone does not
pages.title: Emirates has the strongest all-round Gulf system today, conditional on Dubai, yield and aircraft
points: Emirates carried 53.2 million passengers in the year to March 2026, 11.4 million more than Qatar Airways, and Dubai stayed the world's busiest international airport.
It earned AED19.7bn after tax, a 15.0% margin against 1-3% before the pandemic, because yield rose 53% in ten years while unit cost rose 30%.
The volume lead is narrowing: Emirates is the only one of five hub carriers still below its 2018 passenger count, and Doha and Abu Dhabi outgrew Dubai.
The 2026 shock hit Dubai hardest - DXB seats were still 15% down in September - and 270 777X are on order with none yet flying.

points.text: Emirates reported 152 directly served cities in 80 countries and territories at 31 March 2026; the five routes drawn reach Europe, the Americas, Australasia, Africa and South Asia without a second hub, as examples of that reach.
At March 2026 Emirates had 32 codeshare and 117 interline partners; by September it cited 168 partnerships adding about 1,750 onward cities, reached through the same Dubai connections.

A line hides frequency, so a daily and a thrice-daily service look the same; itinerary quality depends on timing, connection, seats and fare, which need a dated schedule test on each route before any network claim is ranked.

paragraphs: Qatar Airways is the rival that most nearly matches Emirates' model: one global hub, a widebody fleet and a premium product. On service it leads, second in the world and first in the Middle East on Skytrax's 2026 ranking, with the business-class and Wi-Fi awards. On reach it publishes more than 160 summer gateways against Emirates' 152 operated cities, though on different dates and definitions.

On scale the order reverses. In the year to March 2026 Emirates carried 53.2 million passengers against Qatar's 41.8 million, and Qatar's count fell about 3% on the year. To close that gap in three years with Emirates standing still, Qatar would need about 8.4% growth a year.

Qatar has also grown faster. Its passengers are 42% above their 2018 level while Emirates' are 9% below, and Doha's airport traffic is 40% above 2019 against Dubai's 10%. If that pace resumes after the 2026 shock, the scale lead is a question of years rather than decades.

So Qatar is the countercase for a premium traveller choosing a cabin, not for an investor judging the system. The deck returns to that split in section 05, where the preferred airline changes with the decision being made.

pages.title: Etihad is growing fastest: 21% more capacity, fuller aircraft and more seats in 2026

blocks.label: Capacity growing fastest
points: Etihad grew seat capacity 21% to 111.5bn seat-km in 2025, while Emirates' capacity fell 1%.
It still flies under a third of Emirates' 356bn, so the threat is growth, not size.

blocks.label: It fills its seats
points: Its 88.3% load factor is ten points fuller than Emirates' 78.4%: Etihad sold its extra seats rather than flying them empty.
Fuller aircraft spread each flight's cost over more passengers, the lever a smaller hub has when it cannot match Emirates' premium yield.

blocks.label: Profitable at half the margin
points: Etihad earned AED2.6bn after tax on AED30.7bn of revenue, an 8.4% margin, about half of Emirates' 15.0%.
This growth comes with a profit, unlike Etihad's loss-making expansion of the late 2010s.

blocks.label: Still growing in 2026
points: Etihad's September 2026 seats are 11% above a year earlier while Emirates' are 10% below.
Abu Dhabi's airport seats are up 9.8% while Dubai's are down 15.2%, so Etihad is taking traffic while Dubai rebuilds.

points.lead: Three can be watched, not forecast
points.text: A reversal on traffic, margin or connectivity would show first in a published result, so each is read at its date rather than forecast now; none is near its trigger today.
The 777X is 270 of 367 aircraft on order, and Boeing's 2027 aim is not an Emirates date, so A350 and 787 deliveries set growth until one is flying.
DXB fell to 31st on OAG's global index and Emirates' September seats were 9.9% below 2025, so the 2027 readings will show whether the shock was temporary or a loss of share.
With AED54.9bn of cash and net debt of AED1.3bn, none of the four checks turns on financing: each turns on traffic, yield or Boeing.

pages.why: The close restates the answer as the conditions a reader should watch, one to an item
pages.title: Emirates is best positioned to lead, if execution matches the assets
items: Emirates leads the Gulf on scale, profit and hub traffic today: 53.2m passengers, AED19.7bn after tax at a 15.0% margin, and the world's busiest international airport.
Watch Dubai's recovery first: DXB seats were still 15% down in September 2026 while Abu Dhabi and Riyadh grew, and IATA expects the region to lose US$4.3bn this year.
Watch premium yield next: yield rose 4.1% in FY2025-26, but Qatar holds the 2026 business-class awards that decide premium fares.
Watch the fleet last and longest: 270 777X are on order with none flying, so A350s and retrofits must bridge any further slip.
Re-test the case at each dated check - May 2027, May 2028, OAG 2027 and March 2030 - rather than treating today's lead as permanent.
